content: Iron(III) oxide, also referred to as ferric oxide, hematite, red iron oxide, synthetic maghemite, colcothar, or simply rust, is one of the various oxide compounds of iron. It exhibits paramagnetic properties and has the chemical formula Fe₂O₃. Different Forms of Iron(III) Oxide Alpha Phase (α-Fe₂O₃) The alpha phase of iron(III) oxide has a rhombohedral crystal structure, similar to corundum (α-Al₂O₃), and is the most common form. It naturally occurs as the mineral hematite, which is extensively mined as the primary ore of iron. This phase is antiferromagnetic up to its critical temperature of 950 K. It can be synthesized through thermal decomposition or precipitation in the liquid phase. Factors such as pressure, particle size, and magnetic field intensity can influence its properties. Beta Phase The beta phase of iron(III) oxide has a cubic face-centered structure and is metastable. At temperatures above 500°C, it transitions to the alpha phase. It can be prepared by reducing hematite with carbon, pyrolyzing iron(III) chloride solutions, or thermally decomposing iron(III) sulfate. Gamma Phase The gamma phase of iron(III) oxide has a cubic structure and is also metastable, converting to the alpha phase at elevated temperatures. It naturally occurs as the mineral maghemite and exhibits ferrimagnetic properties. Ultrafine particles smaller than 10 nanometers in this phase are superparamagnetic. This phase can be synthesized by thermally dehydrating gamma iron(III) oxide-hydroxide, carefully oxidizing iron(II,III) oxide, or thermally decomposing iron(III) oxalate. Epsilon Phase The epsilon phase of iron(III) oxide has a rhombic structure and displays properties intermediate between the alpha and gamma phases. It has not been isolated in pure form and is typically mixed with either the alpha or gamma phases. Materials with a high proportion of the epsilon phase can be prepared by thermally transforming the gamma phase. The epsilon phase is metastable and transitions to the alpha phase at temperatures between 500°C and 750°C. It can also be synthesized by oxidizing iron in an electric arc or through sol-gel precipitation from iron(III) nitrate. Other Phases Iron(III) oxide can also exist in high-pressure or amorphous forms. Applications of Iron(III) Oxide Magnetic Storage Iron(III) oxide is widely used in magnetic storage media, such as the magnetic layer of floppy disks. These disks consist of a thin PET film coated with iron(III) oxide particles, which can be magnetized to represent binary data. Magnetic ink character recognition (MICR) also employs iron(III) oxide compounds suspended in ink, which can be read by specialized scanning hardware. The majority of recorded information on Earth, including text and photographs, is stored as magnetization patterns on thin layers of iron(III) oxide. This is due to the low cost per bit of iron-based magnetic media compared to alternatives like optical discs, paper books, or microfilm. Polishing A finely powdered form of ferric oxide, known as jeweler's rouge, red rouge, or simply rouge, is used for polishing metallic jewelry and lenses. Historically, it was also used as a cosmetic. Rouge cuts more slowly than modern polishes like cerium(IV) oxide but is still favored in optics fabrication and jewelry-making for the superior finish it produces. When polishing gold, rouge slightly stains the metal, enhancing the appearance of the finished piece. Rouge is available as a powder, paste, polishing cloths, or solid bars bound with wax or grease. Residual rouge on jewelry is typically removed using ultrasonic cleaning. Chemical Applications Iron(III) oxide is used in the production of pure iron in blast furnaces. It is also a key reactant in the highly exothermic thermite reaction, which is represented by the equation: 2 Al + Fe₂O₃ → 2 Fe + Al₂O₃. Pigments Iron(III) oxide serves as a pigment under names such as Pigment Brown 6, Pigment Brown 7, and Pigment Red 101. Some of these pigments, like Pigment Red 101 and Pigment Brown 6, are approved by the FDA for use in cosmetics. Biomedical Applications Nanoparticles of iron(III) oxide are biocompatible, non-toxic, chemically active on their surface, and magnetic. These properties make them highly useful in biomedical applications. They are employed as contrast agents in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), for labeling cancerous tissues, in magnetically controlled drug delivery, in localized thermotherapy (where tissues labeled with iron oxide nanoparticles are heated using an AC magnetic field), and in the preparation of ferrofluids.
